03 / FROM SCAN TO PREDICTION

A compact geometric model, learned from fit outcomes.

Measure the face

Turn selected 3D landmark pairs into distances. Average recent samples and sum nose, cheek and chin paths.

→
Compare each mask

Calculate facial path perimeter minus mask perimeter. Identify its fit family, style and strap type.

→
Score & rank

Apply coefficients learned from fit / not-fit labels, convert to a 0–1 score, and rank candidate masks.

Key assumption: perimeter mismatch captures enough relevant geometry to help prioritize options.

The current score compresses four facial path lengths into one total. It does not simulate a mask deforming or sealing against a full 3D face.

Sources: MasqFit measurement code; FacialMeasurement aggregation; custom_lr preparation, calc_preds and inference path. Score calibration remains a validation question.

APPENDIX A / OUTCOME LABELS

Several evidence paths feed a fit / not-fit label.

Evidence sourceProject labeling rule
Direct N95-mode quantitative testAggregate exercise fit factors; label pass at ≥100.
N99-mode quantitative testEstimate leakage using filtration data; aggregate and apply the project’s ×2 adjustment; label pass at ≥100.
Qualitative fit testUse recorded exercise outcomes, subject to the service’s missing-result handling.
User seal checkFailure → negative label. Passing or incomplete check → no label from this source.
“Fit” here is a data label. Preserve whether it was measured, inferred, or reported.

When sources disagree for the same record ID, current consolidation prioritizes a negative label. Unlabeled records are excluded by default.

Sources: N95ModeService; N99ModeToN95ModeConverterService; QlftService; UserSealCheckService; FitTestsWithFacialMeasurementsService.
APPENDIX B / TWO MEASUREMENT MODES

The same ratio, different particles counted.

Fit factor = outside particle concentration / inside particle concentration

N99 mode / standard mode

Counts a broad aerosol size range. The in-mask count can reflect both filter penetration and leakage.

With sufficiently efficient filters, penetration contributes less and the ratio is more specific to fit.

N95 mode / N95-Companion

Selects a narrow band of negatively charged particles, nominally around 55 nm, that suitable respirator filters capture efficiently.

Reducing the filter-penetration contribution makes the measurement more specific to leakage.

Mode names describe the measurement method; they do not certify a mask as N95 or N99.
Sources: TSI RFT-007; N95-Companion performance study. Exact particle selection varies with instrument design.
APPENDIX C / N95-MODE SAMPLING

Select particles in the instrument’s sample stream.

Sample

Use a mask probe and an ambient inlet. Switch between samples, allowing the lines to purge.

→
Select & count

The classifier selects particles by electrical mobility. The condensation particle counter measures their concentration.

→
Compare

Compare outside and inside concentrations during the prescribed fit-test exercises.

Why this helps N95-class filters

It reduces false fit failures caused by particles penetrating acceptable filter media.

Keep the interpretation specific

The mode estimates fit; it is not a filter-certification test or an all-particle protection factor.

Room air is not prefiltered before the wearer breathes it. Use the supported respirator category, instrument checks and prescribed protocol.

Sources: TSI sampling manual; TSI RFT-007. A generic “≥95%” measurement alone does not establish instrument compatibility.
APPENDIX D / FILTRATION DATA & CREDIT

Estimate what gets through the filter itself.

Aaron Collins (“MaskNerd”)

Credit to Aaron Collins of OpenAeros for contributed filtration-efficiency data used by the project.

Imported entries identified as Aaron’s data are one source. Source measurements are not proof of fit for another wearer.

Aaron Collins · OpenAeros

Contributed sealed measurements

An optional N99-mode “Normal breathing (SEALED)” observation estimates penetration with face-seal gaps minimized.

Residual leakage, breathing flow, aerosol conditions and mask variation can affect this estimate.

Sealed ratio S = 1 / (1 − E)   ·   E = filtration efficiency as a fraction

Example: E = 98% → S = 50. The code pools available sealed ratios by mask using an arithmetic mean.

Source: N99ModeToN95ModeConverterService.avg_sealed_ffs_sql; project dashboard description. Mean of sealed ratios is not mean filtration efficiency.
APPENDIX E / THE CONVERSION MODEL

Separate filter penetration from inferred leakage.

A simplified mixture

Let F be the observed N99-mode ratio, E the estimated filtration efficiency, and L the fraction entering through leaks.

1/F = L + (1 − L)(1 − E)

Assumes leakage admits ambient particles and the filtered stream has penetration 1 − E, under comparable sampling conditions.

Solve for leakage

L = 1 − (1 − 1/F) / E
Estimated leakage fit factor = 1/L

This is the core mathematical estimate. The production labeling formula adds project-specific adjustments.

Illustrative: E = 98%, F = 25 → L ≈ 2.04% → estimated leakage fit factor ≈ 49.

As F approaches the sealed reference, the estimate becomes highly sensitive to measurement error.

Equation derivation: inferring-n95-mode-fit-factors.ipynb ↗

Derivation: project notebook inferring-n95-mode-fit-factors.ipynb and converter implementation. Illustration, not participant data or an instrument equivalence claim.
APPENDIX F / WHAT THE CODE ACTUALLY DOES

From the leakage estimate to the stored label.

  1. Choose a sealed reference. Average available sealed ratios S. If the largest exercise ratio is ≥S, replace S with that maximum + 1.
  2. Convert each eligible exercise. Set E = 1 − 1/S; compute 1 / [1 − (1 − 1/F) / E]. Exclude “Talking” and the sealed reference exercise.
  3. Aggregate and adjust. Take the harmonic mean of the converted factors, multiply by 2, then label pass at ≥100.
Stored estimate = 2 × n / Σ(1 / converted exercise factor)

If every exercise in the illustrative example gives 49, the stored estimate is 98 → fail.

The notebook calls ×2 a sensitivity-oriented bias adjustment. It is not part of the physical derivation or the direct N95 measurement.

Source: converter service and project notebook. These adjustments require validation; inferred results remain a distinct evidence source.
APPENDIX G / USER SEAL CHECKS

Failure supplies a negative signal; a pass is not proof.

Failed check

“Too big,” “Too small,” or a completed response reporting “A lot of air movement.”

→ not-fit label

An inferred negative outcome, not a newly performed formal fit test.

Passed check

No reported failure under the questionnaire’s criteria.

→ no positive fit label

The check cannot establish that a formal fit test would pass.

Incomplete check

Missing or uninterpretable required answers.

→ unknown

No label from this source; another recorded test may provide one.

In this dataset: user seal check fail → failed-fit label.
User seal check pass ⇏ successful fit test.
Sources: UserSealCheckService.qlft_pass_value and consolidation service. A formal test remains separate from a user seal check.

APPENDIX I / WHAT GPL-3 MEANS

The freedom to inspect, improve and carry it forward.

Use & inspect

Run the software, study its source, and evaluate how the methods work. Commercial use is permitted.

Modify & share

Adapt or fork the code. Distributed covered derivatives must preserve GPL-3 freedoms and license terms.

Provide source

When distributing covered binaries, provide recipients access to the corresponding source under the license’s rules.

Practical advantages: auditable methods, independent experimentation, and continuity if the original maintainer steps away.

GPL-3 covers the software; it does not automatically make participant data public. Private changes and merely running a hosted service do not generally trigger a public-source release obligation.

Sources: Breathesafe LICENSE; MasqFit LICENSE.md; GNU GPLv3 guide. Plain-language summary; the full license governs.

APPENDIX K / COORDINATES → DISTANCES

Measure selected segments of the facial mesh.

1. Landmark coordinates

ARKit provides indexed 3D vertices. The app selects predefined pairs along fit-relevant facial paths.

Point i = (xᵢ, yᵢ, zᵢ)

2. Euclidean segment lengths

dᵢⱼ = √[(xᵢ−xⱼ)² + (yᵢ−yⱼ)² + (zᵢ−zⱼ)²]

Compute each pair’s length per sample, then average the recent lengths. Convert meters to millimeters.

The current measurement engine averages the last 10 samples. The controller normally collects 30 updates before auto-stopping.

Assumptions: stable landmark correspondence, meaningful scale and a steady scan. Averaging can reduce fluctuation; it cannot remove systematic measurement bias.

Sources: FacialLandmarks.distance; MeasurementEngine.getAverageMeasurements / exportMeasurements; FaceMeasurementViewController. Local code review, not an instrument accuracy study.
APPENDIX L / DISTANCES → A PERIMETER PROXY

Five aggregates are collected; four enter the score.

AggregateConstructionCurrent fit score
Nose8 predefined segment lengthsIncluded in perimeter total
Upper cheek14 segment lengthsIncluded in perimeter total
Mid-cheek10 segment lengthsIncluded in perimeter total
Chin14 segment lengthsIncluded in perimeter total
Strap-related facial path8 segment lengthsCollected; not used by current score
Pface = nose + upper cheek + mid-cheek + chin

These are sums of short 3D chords along chosen paths, not a full head circumference or a contact-pressure measurement.

Sources: FacialMeasurement.aggregated_arkit_measurements; FacialAggregates; train.py FACIAL_MEASUREMENTS and prep_data_in_torch_with_categories.
APPENDIX M / THE ACTUAL SCORING EQUATION

A quadratic mismatch model with a logistic output.

Δ = (Pface, mm − Pmask, mm) / 10   ·   score = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))
z = (afamily + astyle)Δ² + (bfamily + bstyle)Δ
  + cfamily + cstyle + sstrap type

Family: related variants

A project-assigned fit group. Example: Trident Small in white and black sharing one family (illustrative grouping).

Style: overall shape

Examples: Boat (trifold), Bifold, Cup and Duckbill.

Strap type: attachment

Headstrap or Earloop, with separate Adjustable categories. This is not the facial strap-path length.

Family and style each supply curvature, slope and intercept; strap type adds an offset.
New training constrains curvature with a = −exp(raw parameter).

Sources: train.py; mask form categories; fit-family summary spec (Trident example, not verified catalog assignment). Legacy parameter files need not enforce the new curvature constraint.
APPENDIX N / WHAT THE CURVE ASSUMES

Each family / style favors a range of mismatch.

A mask can prefer a nonzero difference: the learned linear term shifts the peak.
Negative curvature penalizes moving far enough to either side of that preferred difference.

For a fixed mask and strap type, two faces with the same summed perimeter receive the same score.

Schematic generated from the model equation using invented coefficients. It does not characterize any actual mask or measured probability.
APPENDIX O / LEARNING FROM OUTCOMES

Fit the coefficients, then score a new face.

Build training rows

Join measurements, mask metadata and fit / not-fit labels. Some missing scan aggregates are estimated from traditional measurements.

→
Learn parameters

Optimize binary cross-entropy on labeled rows using Adam. Evaluate with user-grouped splits.

→
Serve recommendations

Use saved parameters and mask metadata to compute scores for candidate masks; return them in descending score order.

The model learns associations with the constructed outcome labels. It inherits their measurement error, selection effects and source differences.

Grouping the fit-model split by user is helpful, but end-to-end evaluation must also assess imputation and preprocessing within the split.

Sources: train_custom_lr_with_split; predict_arkit_from_traditional; inference MaskRecommenderInference. Class reweighting is optional; current Rails training defaults leave it off.
APPENDIX P / ASSUMPTIONS & LIMITATIONS

What this compact model captures—and leaves out.

Geometry compression

One perimeter proxy carries the facial signal. Different nose/chin proportions with the same total are indistinguishable to this score.

Shared effects

Fit-family and style effects add together; strap type shifts the score. Actual strap tension, deformation and donning technique are not simulated.

Data transfer

Labels, imputed measurements and contributed users must generalize to new people. Repeated observations can give some users more influence.

Score interpretation

A sigmoid supplies a 0–1 score, not automatic calibration or uncertainty. Breathability and demographics are not direct inputs to this scoring equation.

Next validation targets: scan repeatability, perimeter compression, imputation, unknown-mask behavior and prospective fit outcomes.

Assumptions inferred from the inspected custom_lr computation. Broader feature utilities exist in the repository but are not all consumed by this model.
